author: Rev Fab fire
dailyPrayer: Lord God, on this holy Sunday we bow before You in awe and gratitude, for Your mercies are new every morning and Your faithfulness stretches beyond the horizon of our understanding. We ask that You open our eyes to see Your hand at work in every detail of this day, and that You soften our hearts to receive whatever word You have prepared for us. Where there is weariness, breathe in Your strength; where there is doubt, fan the flame of faith; where there is division, pour out the oil of Your peace. Let this day be more than a ritual — let it be a true encounter with the living God, a moment that transforms us from the inside out. We offer You our praise, our burdens, and our whole selves as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable in Your sight. Amen.

wordOfTheDay.meaning: Repentance, or literally 'turning back' — a complete reorientation of the heart, mind, and will toward God. It is not merely regret for sin but a decisive turning away from it and a wholehearted return to the Lord.
wordOfTheDay.verse: Joel 2:13 — "Rend your heart and not your garments. Return to the LORD your God, for He is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and abounding in love."
wordOfTheDay.reflection: Teshuvah is one of the most beautiful concepts in all of Scripture because it declares that no one is ever too far gone to come home. No matter how many times we have strayed, the Father's arms remain open and His welcome remains warm. Today, let teshuvah be more than a word — let it be an act: turn your face toward God, release what has held you back, and step into the freedom of His embrace.

shortSermon.title: The Power of Turning: Why Teshuvah Changes Everything
shortSermon.scripture: Luke 15:20 — "But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him."
shortSermon.body:
There is a moment in the parable of the prodigal son that we often rush past — the moment the son 'came to himself.' He was sitting in a pigsty, far from home, starving on husks meant for animals, when something shifted deep inside him. He remembered who he was and whose he was. That moment of remembrance, that pivot of the soul, is what the Hebrew calls teshuvah — a turning back. And it is the hinge on which the entire story swings.

The Hebrew word teshuvah comes from the root shuv, meaning to turn or to return. It appears over a thousand times in the Old Testament, and every time it carries the same urgent, hopeful call: you do not have to stay where you are. God is not a distant deity waiting to punish you for your failures; He is a Father who has been scanning the horizon for the first sign of your return. The prophet Joel does not say 'clean yourself up and then come back.' He says 'rend your heart' — come broken, come empty, come as you are — and discover a God who is gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, and abounding in love.

This is the radical grace of teshuvah: the turning does not have to be perfect to be real. The prodigal did not arrive home with a polished speech and a clean conscience — he arrived rehearsing an apology, fully expecting to be demoted to a servant. But the father did not wait for the speech. He ran. In the ancient Near East, a dignified patriarch did not run; it was considered undignified. Yet this father hiked up his robes and sprinted down the road because his child was coming home. That is the God we serve. That is the welcome that awaits every soul who turns.

I want to speak to someone today who has been living in a far country — not necessarily a physical place, but a spiritual one. Perhaps you have drifted from your first love, grown cold in prayer, or carried a secret burden of shame for so long that you have forgotten what freedom feels like. Teshuvah is your invitation. You do not need a grand gesture or a perfect plan — you simply need to turn. Turn your face toward the Father, take one step in His direction, and watch Him close the distance. Let us pray together: Father, we turn to You today. Receive us, restore us, and remind us that we are Yours. In Jesus' name, Amen.
